Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BOSTON, Massachusetts (CNN)  -- Timothy Connick was in agony for six years. In bed at night, it felt as if a pair of scissors was sticking out of his foot. "I turn over, and it's just like they're getting jammed in more." Timothy Connick got relief from chronic pain through a peripheral nerve stimulator implanted above his hip. Connick, 52 from Lynn, Massachusetts, injured his foot falling from a loading dock at work 11 years ago. "I fell about seven feet onto the concrete and smashed my heel. It started hurting that moment and kept hurting for six years after that." Connick is among millions. As many as one in three American adults suffer from chronic pain, according to the American Chronic Pain Association. The organization defines chronic pain as "pain that continues a month or more beyond the usual recovery period for an injury or illness or that goes on for months or years because of a chronic condition."  It's usually not constant, the group says, but can disrupt the sufferer's life. Over the years, Connick consulted multiple doctors and tried two dozen medications for pain management, but nothing eased the pain and the resulting depression. "It was pretty much a no-win situation as long as that pain was going to be there," he recalls. He was eventually referred to neurologist Anne Louise Oaklander, director of the nerve injury unit at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston. "Pain is the No. 1 reason why patients seek medical care, but until recently it hasn't been part of the medical school curriculum," she says. "Many physicians and nurses feel uncomfortable and unqualified to treat these patients." Oaklander sees many patients whom she describes as "bouncing around the health care system" for years with no firm diagnosis. She divides chronic pain sufferers into two groups. "One is the group that has an ongoing cause of their pain," she says. "The classic example of that is patients with arthritis. They have pain in their joints every day." Much more difficult, she says, is the second group: "Patients who have chronic pain without an obvious cause of tissue injury." Connick falls in the second category, Oaklander says, noting that X-rays show broken bones, but not nerve damage. "It was only many years later when he was examined by a neurologist that his underlying nerve injury was identified and able to be treated," she said.  Health Minute: The struggle of managing chronic pain » . Oaklander says pain medications can help most patients, but there are other options. For instance, she says, if the pain is related to an orthopedic problem, physical therapy may be the best choice. In Connick's case, relief came through surgery to implant a peripheral nerve stimulator above his hip. Based on pacemaker technology, the stimulator is placed under the skin and works by giving off benign pulses that override pain signals to the brain, Oaklander explains. She cautions that minor surgery is involved, and the device works in only about half the patients who get it. For Connick, it made all the difference. "The day they put it in and I turned it on, I was up seven flights of stairs before they stopped me. Everything that I hadn't been able to do and everything that made me happy was back available to me again and I knew it right away." These days, Connick is back at work loading trucks. He's on his feet all day and doesn't complain about any pain. Oaklander concludes: "If you have chronic pain, don't take no for an answer....I think it's important for chronic pain patients to keep a sense of purpose, optimism and hope despite the indignities that many are subjected to." E-mail to a friend . Judy Fortin is a correspondent with CNN Medical News. Linda Ciampa of Accent Health contributed to this report.

BOSTON, Massachusetts (CNN) — For six years, Timothy Connick lived with excruciating pain. At night, he felt as though scissors were protruding from his foot and were being pushed in deeper whenever he rolled over in bed.

Connick, a 52-year-old resident of Lynn, Massachusetts, eventually found relief after doctors implanted a peripheral nerve stimulator above his hip.

His ordeal began 11 years earlier, when he fell approximately seven feet from a loading dock while working. He landed on concrete and crushed his heel. The pain began immediately and continued for the next six years.

Connick is one of millions of people affected by long-term pain. According to the American Chronic Pain Association, chronic pain may affect as many as one-third of U.S. adults. The group describes it as pain that remains for at least a month beyond the normal healing time for an illness or injury, or persists for months or years because of an ongoing medical condition. Although it is generally not continuous, the organization says it can still seriously interfere with a person’s daily life.

During those years, Connick saw numerous doctors and used about 24 different pain medications. None relieved either his physical suffering or the depression it caused. He remembers feeling that there could be no positive outcome as long as the pain continued.

Eventually, he was sent to neurologist Anne Louise Oaklander, who leads the nerve injury unit at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston. Oaklander says pain is the leading reason people seek medical treatment, yet it was not included in medical school training until relatively recently. As a result, she says, many doctors and nurses do not feel sufficiently prepared or comfortable caring for patients with chronic pain.

Oaklander frequently treats people who have spent years moving from one part of the health care system to another without receiving a definite diagnosis. She places chronic pain patients into two broad categories.

The first consists of those whose pain has a continuing, identifiable source. Arthritis is a typical example, because affected patients experience joint pain every day.

The second category is far more challenging, Oaklander says. It includes people who suffer persistent pain even though there is no clear evidence of ongoing tissue damage.

According to Oaklander, Connick belonged to this second group. X-rays can reveal fractures, she explains, but they cannot show injured nerves. His underlying nerve damage was not discovered until many years later, when a neurologist examined him. Once it was identified, doctors were able to treat it.

The report also included a “Health Minute” feature about the difficulties of controlling chronic pain.

Oaklander says medication is effective for most patients, but it is not the only possible treatment. When pain stems from an orthopedic condition, for example, physical therapy may be the most appropriate approach.

For Connick, the answer was surgery to place a peripheral nerve stimulator beneath the skin above his hip. The device is derived from pacemaker technology. It produces harmless electrical pulses that interrupt or override pain messages traveling to the brain, Oaklander says.

She notes that implantation requires a minor operation and that the treatment is successful in only about half of the patients who receive the device.

For Connick, however, the results were transformative. On the day the stimulator was implanted, he switched it on and climbed seven flights of stairs before staff members stopped him. He immediately realized that the activities he had lost—and the things that had once brought him happiness—were available to him again.

Connick has since returned to his job loading trucks. He spends the entire workday standing and no longer reports pain.

Oaklander advises people with chronic pain not to accept a refusal to help as the final answer. She believes such patients should hold on to purpose, optimism and hope, despite the humiliating experiences many endure.

The original report included an option to e-mail the story to a friend. Judy Fortin, a correspondent for CNN Medical News, reported the piece, with contributions from Linda Ciampa of Accent Health.

Chronic pain affects millions of Americans, yet it remains difficult to diagnose and treat. Patients may spend years trying medications, physical therapy, injections, surgery, and other interventions without finding lasting relief. The challenge is especially acute when pain persists after an injury has healed or when routine tests fail to reveal a clear cause.

Timothy Connick experienced this problem firsthand. For six years, he lived with severe pain in his foot that did not respond to conventional medications. The pain interfered with his daily life and continued despite repeated efforts to control it. Like many people with treatment-resistant pain, Connick had exhausted the standard options available to him.

Neurologist Anne Louise Oaklander pursued a more targeted approach. Rather than relying on drugs that act throughout the body, she used an implanted peripheral nerve stimulator designed to influence the specific nerves carrying pain signals from Connick’s foot. The device delivers controlled electrical impulses near the affected nerve, altering the abnormal signals before they reach the brain and are experienced as pain.

For Connick, the treatment provided relief after years of suffering. His experience illustrates the potential of peripheral nerve stimulation for carefully selected patients whose pain is linked to identifiable nerves and has not improved with less invasive treatments.

The procedure is not a universal cure, and implanted stimulators carry potential risks, including infection, device problems, and inadequate pain relief. Patients must undergo a thorough evaluation to determine whether nerve stimulation is appropriate. Nevertheless, Connick’s case shows how advances in neurology and pain medicine can offer hope when conventional therapies have failed.

Targeted nerve stimulation also reflects a broader shift in chronic-pain care: treating pain according to its underlying biological mechanisms rather than relying solely on systemic medication. For patients with severe, localized, medication-resistant pain, this approach may provide a path back to greater comfort and function.

# A loading-dock injury left him in relentless pain. A nerve specialist helped uncover why

**By Health News Desk**

A routine shift at a loading dock changed Timothy Connick’s life.

After being injured at work, Connick expected the pain to ease as his body healed. Instead, it persisted, spreading beyond what doctors might ordinarily expect from the original injury. Everyday movement became difficult, and the pain continued long after the initial tissue damage should have improved.

His case eventually brought him to Dr. Anne Louise Oaklander, a neurologist and nerve-injury researcher at Massachusetts General Hospital. Oaklander’s work focuses on patients whose chronic pain may be driven by damage to the body’s small nerve fibers—delicate nerves that carry pain and temperature signals and help regulate functions such as sweating, blood pressure and heart rate.

Testing indicated that Connick’s symptoms were not simply psychological or an exaggerated response to an old injury. His nervous system itself appeared to be malfunctioning.

That distinction can be life-changing for patients who have spent years being told that routine scans and blood tests are normal.

## When pain outlasts the injury

Chronic pain generally refers to pain that lasts longer than three months. It affects millions of Americans and can interfere with sleep, employment, mobility and mental health.

Unlike acute pain—the body’s short-term alarm after an injury—chronic pain may continue after tissues have healed. In some patients, injured peripheral nerves keep sending abnormal signals. In others, the spinal cord and brain become more sensitive, amplifying sensations that would not ordinarily hurt.

Oaklander has argued that some difficult-to-explain pain syndromes may involve small-fiber neuropathy, which does not always appear on conventional nerve-conduction studies. Doctors may instead use a neurological examination, autonomic testing or a small skin biopsy to measure nerve-fiber density.

For Connick, identifying a possible biological source opened the door to treatment directed at the damaged or dysregulated nerves rather than relying only on painkillers. His care under Oaklander included a specialist-guided approach based on the suspected nerve disorder and its underlying cause.

Not every patient responds the same way, and treatments sometimes used in immune-associated neuropathies—including intravenous immunoglobulin—carry risks, are expensive and remain controversial for some chronic-pain conditions. They are not routine therapies for chronic pain and should be considered only after careful evaluation by qualified specialists.

## A broader shift in pain medicine

Connick’s experience illustrates a change in how medicine views chronic pain: It is not always merely a lingering symptom. In some people, it becomes a disease process involving the nervous or immune system.

Treatment often requires multiple strategies, including physical rehabilitation, medications targeted to nerve pain, psychological support, sleep care and treatment of any underlying medical condition. Opioids may help selected patients, but they bring risks of tolerance, dependence and overdose and are generally not a complete long-term solution.

Experts also caution that a normal MRI or X-ray does not mean a patient’s pain is imaginary. Many pain-generating abnormalities are microscopic or functional and cannot be seen on standard imaging.

Connick’s case does not offer a universal cure. But it underscores why persistent pain deserves a thorough medical investigation—and why, for some patients, finding the injured nerves behind the pain can be the first step toward reclaiming their lives.

# Chronic pain is common, costly — and often difficult to diagnose and treat

**By Staff Writer**

For millions of people, pain does not end when an injury heals or an illness is treated. It continues for months or years, disrupting sleep, employment, mobility and family life while frequently eluding a clear diagnosis.

The American Chronic Pain Association, citing a landmark Institute of Medicine analysis, has long highlighted an estimate that chronic pain affects more than 100 million Americans and generates between **$560 billion and $635 billion a year** in medical expenses and lost productivity. More recent federal estimates use narrower definitions: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported that approximately **51.6 million U.S. adults — 20.9% of the adult population — experienced chronic pain in 2021**, including 17.1 million whose pain frequently limited work or daily activities.

The difference illustrates one of the central problems in pain medicine: Even measuring chronic pain depends on how it is defined. Most clinicians describe it as pain lasting or recurring for more than three months, but studies vary in whether they count intermittent symptoms, condition-specific pain or pain that significantly restricts daily life.

## No single test can measure pain

Unlike blood pressure or blood glucose, pain cannot be confirmed by one laboratory value or imaging scan. Diagnosis relies heavily on a patient’s description of where the pain occurs, how it feels, what triggers it and how it affects function.

Imaging may identify arthritis, a herniated disc or tissue damage, but those findings do not always explain symptom severity. Some people have substantial abnormalities on scans with little discomfort; others experience disabling pain despite normal or inconclusive imaging.

Pain specialists generally divide chronic pain into overlapping categories:

- **Nociceptive pain**, associated with ongoing tissue injury or inflammation, as in osteoarthritis.
- **Neuropathic pain**, caused by damage or disease affecting nerves, such as diabetic neuropathy.
- **Nociplastic pain**, in which pain-processing pathways appear altered even without clear evidence of tissue damage or nerve injury. Fibromyalgia is a common example.
- **Mixed pain**, involving more than one mechanism.

Determining which mechanism is dominant matters because treatments differ. An anti-inflammatory drug may help an inflamed joint but do little for nerve pain. Surgery can correct a structural problem, yet it may not resolve pain if the nervous system has become sensitized.

Experts also emphasize that describing pain as “biopsychosocial” does not mean it is imaginary. The term recognizes that biological changes interact with sleep, stress, mood, past trauma, work demands, social support and other factors. Anxiety and depression can amplify pain and disability, while persistent pain can itself cause anxiety and depression.

## Delays, disparities and fragmented care

Patients may cycle among primary-care offices, orthopedic surgeons, neurologists, rheumatologists and emergency departments before receiving a useful explanation. Specialists often focus on a particular organ or body region, while chronic pain may involve several conditions at once.

Bias can further complicate assessment. Research has documented disparities in pain evaluation and treatment involving race, sex, age, disability and substance-use history. Because pain is self-reported, patients may feel pressured to prove that their symptoms are real.

Short appointments can also work against careful diagnosis. A thorough evaluation may require review of earlier injuries, surgeries, medications, sleep, mood, physical activity and occupational demands, as well as a neurological and musculoskeletal examination. Clinicians must also rule out urgent causes such as infection, cancer, fractures or spinal-cord compression.

Warning signs requiring prompt medical evaluation can include new weakness, loss of bladder or bowel control, fever, unexplained weight loss, severe pain after trauma or rapidly worsening symptoms.

## Treatment shifts from a “pain score” to function

There is rarely a single cure for long-standing pain. Pain specialists increasingly focus on practical goals: sleeping longer, walking farther, returning to work, caring for children or reducing flare-ups.

The American Chronic Pain Association promotes this self-management approach, encouraging patients to take an active role and to work with clinicians on realistic functional goals rather than expecting one intervention to eliminate all discomfort.

Medication may still be part of treatment. Depending on the condition, clinicians may consider acetaminophen, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, topical treatments, certain antidepressants or anti-seizure medications used for nerve pain. Each has risks, especially when used long term or in patients with other medical conditions.

Opioids remain appropriate for some patients, but they require particular caution. CDC guidance advises clinicians to weigh expected benefits against risks, discuss treatment goals, start with the lowest effective dose when opioids are warranted and avoid abrupt discontinuation in patients already taking them. Long-term use can bring tolerance, physical dependence, constipation, sedation and overdose risk. Physical dependence is not the same as addiction, though opioid-use disorder can occur and should be treated as a medical condition.

## Options beyond medication

For many patients, the strongest approach combines several non-drug therapies tailored to the cause of pain and the person’s circumstances.

Common options include:

- **Physical therapy and graded exercise:** Strength, flexibility and aerobic activity can improve function and reduce fear of movement. Programs generally work best when they begin at a tolerable level and progress gradually.
- **Cognitive behavioral therapy:** CBT helps patients identify thought and behavior patterns that intensify distress and develop coping strategies. It does not imply that pain is “all in the mind.”
- **Acceptance and commitment therapy:** ACT emphasizes pursuing meaningful activities even when symptoms cannot be completely controlled.
- **Mindfulness and relaxation training:** Meditation, breathing exercises and other stress-regulation techniques may reduce pain-related distress and improve quality of life.
- **Occupational therapy:** Therapists can suggest pacing strategies, workplace changes and adaptive equipment to make daily activities more manageable.
- **Sleep treatment:** Addressing insomnia or sleep apnea can be important because poor sleep increases pain sensitivity.
- **Acupuncture, massage or spinal manipulation:** These approaches may provide relief for some conditions and patients, though benefits vary and treatment should be provided by qualified practitioners.
- **Weight management and nutrition support:** When relevant, these may reduce joint load and improve overall health, though they should not be presented as simplistic explanations for pain.
- **Interventional procedures:** Selected patients may benefit from injections, nerve blocks, radiofrequency procedures or implanted stimulation devices. Such treatments should be tied to a specific diagnosis and realistic expectations.
- **Peer support and pain education:** Support groups, including those associated with the American Chronic Pain Association, can reduce isolation and help patients build self-management skills.

Evidence is not equally strong for every therapy, and “natural” does not automatically mean safe. Supplements can interact with prescriptions, while poorly supervised exercise or manipulation may worsen some conditions.

## Access remains a major obstacle

Although clinical guidelines often recommend multidisciplinary care, insurance coverage does not always match those recommendations. Medication may be easier to obtain than repeated physical therapy, behavioral treatment or coordinated pain rehabilitation. Rural communities face shortages of pain specialists, rehabilitation professionals and mental-health providers.

Cost, transportation, caregiving duties and the time required for multiple appointments can also make comprehensive treatment unrealistic. That gap leaves some patients with a choice between medication-only care and no care at all.

Experts in pain medicine argue that successful treatment requires continuity and shared decision-making. A plan should be reassessed for changes in pain, function, side effects and quality of life, rather than continued automatically.

For patients, the process can be slow and frustrating. But clinicians increasingly recognize that improvement does not depend on finding a single hidden injury or a miracle drug. It often comes from identifying the likely pain mechanisms, ruling out dangerous conditions and combining medical care with rehabilitation, psychological support and practical changes that restore as much function as possible.
